title: Spider's web variation
subtitle: A back-stitched or whipped web for a different texture to the woven version
excerpt: The spider's web variation builds a circular motif on the same spoke foundation as a woven web but whips or back-stitches around the spokes instead of weaving over and under, giving a raised ribbed surface.
sourceNotes: Contemporary surface embroidery practice. Variation of the woven spider's web described in Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886).
heroPrompt: Spider's web variation on cream linen, a raised ribbed circular motif worked in rose pink, spokes visible beneath the stitching, close-up, natural light.

content.text: Where the woven spider's web goes over one spoke and under the next, the back-stitch variation works differently. After laying the same odd-number spoke framework, you back-stitch around each spoke, picking up each spoke with a back stitch that wraps around it. The result is a raised ribbed surface rather than the flat woven texture.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton, 2 to 3 strands; the same thread can be used for spokes and working

content.text: Lay the spoke framework: 5 or 7 straight stitches meeting at the centre, evenly spaced around the circle.
Bring the needle up close to the centre. Back-stitch around the first spoke: insert the needle behind it, then bring it up between that spoke and the next.
Continue around the circle, back-stitching each spoke in turn. The needle only enters the fabric occasionally to anchor the working thread; most passes go only around the spokes.
Work outward until the spokes are covered. Finish by inserting the needle into the fabric beside the outer edge of the last row.

items.cause: Pulling the working thread to different tensions on each spoke.
items.fix: Keep consistent moderate tension throughout. The ribs should sit raised but not tight.

items.cause: Spokes unevenly spaced in the foundation.
items.fix: Mark the spoke positions lightly with a water-soluble pen before laying them.

content.text: The back-stitch web adds a raised texture that catches light differently from the flat woven web. Both versions appear in Brazilian embroidery as flower centres and in stumpwork as dimensional circular motifs.
